attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his newsletter, given as his own assessment.

semantics.note: Keeps 'seems' as 'appears' for the OpenAI clause. The startup clause is unhedged and existential. It is a present-state observation, not a forecast.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary. 'At least one' is existential, so any qualifying startup counts, not just the linked White Stork. Treating 'well-funded' as a qualitative word is fair. The contract keeps the weapons limit separate from the opening.

evidence.note: Ars Technica, Jan 17 2024 (before the post): OpenAI dropped its blanket military ban on Jan 10, kept the weapons ban, and works with the DoD. This supports the tentative OpenAI clause.

Shield AI's own Oct 2023 announcement: its Hivemind AI pilot has flown the V-BAT military drone and it is raising money to integrate further. A company disclosure, but adequate for basic product and funding facts.
Shield AI's counsel, Jan 9 2024: $500M total raised in the expanded Series F. This establishes 'well-funded'. It comes from the company's side, not an independent finding.

reviews.rationale: Reporting from before the post shows OpenAI removed its military-use ban and was working with the Pentagon, which fits the hedged 'seems to be opening the door'. Shield AI raised hundreds of millions and was flying its AI pilot on V-BAT military drones, which satisfies the existential startup clause. White Stork's funding is unverified, but the claim does not depend on it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Copied word for word. It is a firm, broad generalization about the state of the technology, with no hedge.

contract.note: 'Seldom dependable across ordinary uses' is a fair, ordinary reading. The contract does not invent a threshold. Without a defined standard for 'rarely' and 'reliable', the result depends on which tasks and standards are chosen.

evidence.note: GenEval (Oct 2023) shows image generators still weak on position and attribute binding and strong on simple tasks. It shows limits, not how often failures happen across uses.
HELM: results depend on the task and method, and it covers an earlier set of language models. It does not settle how common reliable performance was across generative AI in Jan 2024.
MIT experiment: ChatGPT raised average productivity and quality on writing tasks. This counts against the claim, but a higher average is not the same as dependable performance.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows some generative-AI tasks failing and some succeeding, but no representative measure of how often performance was dependable across ordinary uses at publication. The contract asks for exactly that, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence. The scored part is the factual clause about the elephant example.

semantics.note: The revision correctly keeps the 'can't quite' hedge and drops the added word 'simple'. The 'not sure that's a great idea' part is opinion and is correctly left out.

contract.note: Tying the claim to the referenced elephant demonstration and reading 'can't quite' as a demonstrated difficulty is fair. The sentence does not say which example it means, so the contract asks for that to be traced.

evidence.note: Third-party Substack comment saying a different prompt gave better results. It neither verifies the original output nor shows that the original requirements were met.

reviews.rationale: Neither the original elephant prompt nor its output was recovered from an independent record, and Marcus's own post cannot prove itself. The only item is a commenter's unverified report of better results with a changed prompt. The evidence settles neither the support nor the contradiction condition.
